explanation: The spinal cord is cylindrical but flattened anteroposteriorly, extending from foramen magnum to the lower border of L1 vertebra. It has two enlargements (cervical at C5-T1 and lumbar at L2-S3) and shows longitudinal fissures (anterior median fissure and posterior median sulcus). It tapers inferiorly to form the conus medullaris. This shape is clinically important for lumbar puncture and understanding segmental anatomy.
keyConcept: Spinal cord cylindrical shape, flattening, extensions, and conus medullaris

explanation: Spinal nerves exit through intervertebral foramina. Cervical nerves (C1-C7) exit ABOVE their corresponding vertebra. From T1-L1, nerves exit BELOW their corresponding vertebra. Below L1, the cauda equina (L2-S5 nerves) descends in the subarachnoid space before exiting through their respective sacral foramina. This somatotopic arrangement is essential for interpreting segmental neurological deficits.
keyConcept: Spinal nerve exit above/below vertebrae and cauda equina arrangement

explanation: The spinal cord meninges have distinct termination sites: the dura mater ends at the S2 vertebra (forming the dural sac terminus), the arachnoid mater also ends at S2, while the pia mater continues as the filum terminale (a fibrous band) that attaches to the dorsum of the coccyx. Below S2 is the lumbar cistern containing CSF but no spinal cord.
keyConcept: Meninges termination: Dura/Arachnoid at S2, Pia continues as filum terminale to coccyx

explanation: Lumbar puncture is performed to obtain CSF or inject medications. The safe site is between L3-L4 or L4-L5 vertebrae (just above or below the L4 spinous process). The patient is positioned on the side or sitting forward. The needle passes through: skin, superficial fascia, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura mater, and arachnoid mater to reach the subarachnoid space containing CSF.
keyConcept: Lumbar puncture site (L3-L4/L4-L5), layers traversed, and subarachnoid CSF space

explanation: The posterior horn contains four main nuclei: Substantia gelatinosa (lamina II) carries pain and temperature; Nucleus proprius (laminae III, IV) carries touch and pressure; Nucleus dorsalis/Clarke's column (lamina VII) is the origin of spinocerebellar tracts; and the Visceral sensory nucleus receives visceral afferents. These nuclei are the second-order neurons in various sensory pathways.
keyConcept: Four nuclei of posterior horn: substantia gelatinosa, nucleus proprius, nucleus dorsalis, visceral sensory nucleus

explanation: The anterior horn contains motor nuclei organized somatotopically: Medial motor nuclei (medial column) supply muscles of neck and trunk; Lateral motor nuclei (lateral column) supply limb muscles, divided into anterior lateral (sternocleidomastoid, trapezius), posterior lateral (forearm flexors), and postural (limb extensors). The phrenic nucleus at C3,4,5 supplies the diaphragm. These are lower motor neuron cell bodies.
keyConcept: Anterior horn motor nuclei: medial, lateral (with subdivisions), and phrenic nucleus

explanation: The lateral horn exists at two levels with different functions: T1-L2 contains the intermediolateral nucleus (cell column) for preganglionic sympathetic neurons (sympathetic outflow); S2-S4 contains the sacral parasympathetic nucleus for preganglionic parasympathetic neurons (rest and digest function). The lateral horn is absent at other levels.
keyConcept: Lateral horn: sympathetic (T1-L2 via intermediolateral nucleus) and parasympathetic (S2-S4 via sacral parasympathetic nucleus)

explanation: Pain from the face uses the trigeminal pathway: 1st neuron (pseudounipolar) cell body in trigeminal ganglion → enters pons → descends to spinal nucleus of CN V → 2nd neuron decussates as internal arcuate fibers → ascends as trigeminal lemniscus → VPM of thalamus → 3rd neuron projects via posterior limb of internal capsule to postcentral gyrus (S1 cortex).
keyConcept: Trigeminal pain pathway: trigeminal ganglion → spinal nucleus CN V → VPM thalamus → postcentral gyrus

explanation: Pain from the body uses a three-neuron pathway: 1st: Dorsal root ganglion cell (peripheral process receives pain, central process enters spinal cord via Lissauer's tract); 2nd: Substantia gelatinosa/lamina I in posterior horn (axon decussates in anterior white commissure, ascends 1-2 segments); 3rd: VPL nucleus of thalamus (projects to somatosensory cortex via internal capsule).
keyConcept: Three-neuron pain pathway from body: DRG → posterior horn → VPL thalamus → cortex

explanation: Crude touch from the body uses a three-neuron pathway: 1st: Dorsal root ganglion cell (peripheral process receives touch, central process enters and ascends/descends 1-2 segments in Lissauer's tract); 2nd: Nucleus proprius (laminae III, IV) in posterior horn (axon decussates and ascends in ventral spinothalamic tract); 3rd: VPL thalamus → postcentral gyrus. Crude touch crosses early and ascends contralaterally.
keyConcept: Three-neuron crude touch pathway: DRG → nucleus proprius → VPL thalamus → cortex

explanation: Conscious proprioception and fine touch use dorsal column pathways: 1st: Dorsal root ganglion cell (peripheral receptor → central process ascends ipsilaterally in dorsal columns); Gracile tract carries lower body info, cuneate tract carries upper body info. 2nd: Gracile/cuneate nuclei of medulla → internal arcuate fibers decussate → medial lemniscus → VPL thalamus. 3rd: VPL → postcentral gyrus via posterior limb of internal capsule. These fibers remain ipsilateral until the medulla.
keyConcept: Dorsal column pathway: ipsilateral ascent in fasciculus gracilis/cuneatus → medial lemniscus after decussation

explanation: Conscious proprioception is carried by: Gracile tract (lower body below T6) and Cuneate tract (upper body above T6). Unconscious proprioception is carried by: Posterior spinocerebellar tract (from Clarke's nucleus, lower body), Anterior spinocerebellar tract (lower body), and Cuneocerebellar tract (from accessory cuneate nucleus, upper body). The distinction is clinically important.
keyConcept: Conscious: dorsal columns (gracile/cuneate). Unconscious: spinocerebellar tracts (posterior, anterior, cuneocerebellar)

explanation: Unconscious proprioception reaches the cerebellum via spinocerebellar tracts: From lower body: Muscle spindles/Golgi tendon organs → dorsal root ganglion (1st neuron) → Clarke's nucleus in posterior horn (2nd neuron) → posterior spinocerebellar tract → inferior cerebellar peduncle → cerebellum. From upper body: Same pathway but accessory cuneate nucleus → cuneocerebellar tract → inferior cerebellar peduncle. These tracts carry proprioceptive information for motor coordination without conscious awareness.
keyConcept: Unconscious proprioception to cerebellum via spinocerebellar tracts through inferior cerebellar peduncle

explanation: Pain from face and body both reach the thalamus and cortex but use different pathways: BODY: DRG → Lissauer's tract → substantia gelatinosa → decussates → lateral spinothalamic tract → VPL thalamus → postcentral gyrus. FACE: Trigeminal ganglion → spinal nucleus CN V → decussates → trigeminal lemniscus → VPM thalamus → postcentral gyrus. Both pathways converge at thalamus and somatosensory cortex but use different nuclei.
keyConcept: Face pain uses trigeminal lemniscus (VPM); body pain uses spinothalamic tract (VPL)

explanation: Touch from the face is carried by two tracts: Discriminative (fine) touch uses the principal (main) sensory nucleus of CN V → ventral trigeminothalamic tract → VPM of thalamus → postcentral gyrus. Crude touch uses the spinal nucleus of CN V → ventral trigeminothalamic tract → VPM thalamus. Both pathways ultimately project to the VPM and postcentral gyrus.
keyConcept: Face touch: principal sensory nucleus (fine touch) and spinal nucleus (crude touch) both via ventral trigeminothalamic tract to VPM

explanation: The pyramidal tract is somatotopically organized at each level: CEREBRAL CORTEX: Arises from areas 4, 6, and adjacent areas; descends through corona radiata. INTERNAL CAPSULE: Posterior limb (face most anterior, arm, leg most posterior). BRAIN STEM: Basis pedunculi of midbrain (medial 3/5), basis pontis (scattered bundles), medullary pyramids. MEDULLARY DECUSSATION: Arm fibers decussate first (become lateral CST), leg fibers lower. SPINAL CORD: Cervical fibers most medial, sacral most lateral.
keyConcept: Pyramidal tract somatotopy: face anterior in internal capsule, arm medial in cord, leg lateral in cord

explanation: The pyramidal tract terminates on anterior horn cells: The lateral corticospinal tract terminates on alpha motor neurons (final common pathway) and gamma motor neurons in the anterior horn of all spinal segments. The anterior corticospinal tract (uncrossed, small) terminates similarly but only in upper cervical segments. Corticobulbar fibers terminate on cranial nerve motor nuclei in the brainstem.
keyConcept: Corticospinal tract terminates on anterior horn motor neurons; corticobulbar terminates on brainstem motor nuclei

explanation: The corticonuclear (corticobulbar) tract: ORIGIN from precentral/postcentral gyri and frontal eye fields; COURSE through posterior limb of internal capsule, basis pedunculi of midbrain, basis pontis, medullary pyramids; TERMINATION on motor nuclei of cranial nerves (III, IV, V, VI, VII, IX, X, XI, XII). Most CN nuclei receive BILATERAL input except the lower facial nucleus (mainly contralateral) and trochlear nucleus.
keyConcept: Corticobulbar tract: mostly bilateral cortical input to cranial nerve nuclei (except lower face)

explanation: The tectospinal tract: ORIGIN from superior colliculus of midbrain; COURSE decussates immediately below its origin, descends in spinal cord (mostly upper cervical segments); FUNCTION mediates reflex turning of head and neck in response to visual and auditory stimuli (spino-visual and spino-auditory reflexes). It is part of the extrapyramidal system.
keyConcept: Tectospinal tract: superior colliculus origin, immediate decussation, mediates head/neck reflexes to visual/auditory stimuli

explanation: The rubrospinal tract: ORIGIN from red nucleus (magnocellular part) of midbrain; COURSE decussates immediately, descends through brain stem into lateral white column; FUNCTION facilitates flexor muscle tone and inhibits extensor tone; takes over function of corticospinal tract after lesion. Lesion causes decerebrate rigidity.
keyConcept: Rubrospinal tract: red nucleus origin, facilitates flexor tone, takes over after corticospinal lesion

explanation: Blood supply of cervical spinal cord: Anterior spinal artery (from vertebral arteries) supplies anterior 2/3 of cord including anterior horn, lateral horn, anterior and lateral white columns. Posterior spinal arteries (from PICA or vertebral) supply posterior 1/3 including posterior horn and posterior columns. Radicular arteries from vertebral, ascending cervical, and deep cervical arteries reinforce the longitudinal arteries.
keyConcept: Cervical cord blood supply: anterior spinal artery (anterior 2/3) and posterior spinal arteries (posterior 1/3)

explanation: The anterior spinal artery: ORIGIN formed by union of two anterior spinal branches of vertebral arteries at the medulla; COURSE descends in the anterior median fissure; PARTS SUPPLIED: anterior 2/3 of spinal cord, anterior horn (motor), lateral horn (sympathetic), anterior and lateral white columns, and gray commissure with crossing fibers.
keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery: vertebral artery origin, supplies anterior 2/3 of cord including motor and sympathetic regions

explanation: The posterior spinal arteries: ORIGIN usually from posterior inferior cerebellar arteries (PICA) or vertebral arteries; COURSE descends as two vessels near dorsal roots; PARTS SUPPLIED: posterior 1/3 of spinal cord including posterior horn, posterior columns, and posterior white columns. Note: posterior spinal arteries are often discontinuous and depend on radicular artery reinforcement.
keyConcept: Posterior spinal arteries: PICA/vertebral origin, supplies posterior 1/3 (sensory - dorsal columns)

explanation: Arteries giving radicular arteries to spinal cord include: vertebral arteries, ascending cervical arteries (branch of inferior thyroid artery), deep cervical arteries (branch of costocervical trunk), intercostal arteries (for thoracic segments), lumbar arteries (for lumbar segments), and lateral sacral arteries (for sacral segments). These reinforce the longitudinal spinal arteries.
keyConcept: Radicular arteries: vertebral, ascending/deep cervical, intercostal, lumbar, and sacral arteries

explanation: UMN vs LMN lesion differences: UMN lesions cause spastic paralysis, hypertonia, hyperreflexia, clonus, positive Babinski sign, and no muscle atrophy (or minimal). LMN lesions cause flaccid paralysis, hypotonia, hyporeflexia/areflexia, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, and no Babinski sign. UMN affects descending corticospinal pathways; LMN affects the peripheral motor neurons or their cell bodies.
keyConcept: UMN: spastic, hyperreflexia, Babinski positive, no atrophy. LMN: flaccid, areflexia, atrophy, fasciculations

explanation: Two main tracts affected by hemisection of spinal cord: (1) LATERAL CORTICOSPINAL TRACT - ipsilateral UMN paralysis below lesion (controls voluntary movement); (2) SPINOTHALAMIC TRACTS - contralateral loss of pain and temperature (after decussation) below lesion. Posterior columns are also affected (ipsilateral loss of proprioception/fine touch).
keyConcept: Hemisection affects: ipsilateral corticospinal (UMN paralysis) and contralateral spinothalamic (pain/temperature loss)

explanation: Complete transection of spinal cord: IMMEDIATE (spinal shock): flaccid paralysis, loss of all sensations, absent reflexes below lesion. AFTER WEEKS: spastic paralysis, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski. SENSORY: complete loss below lesion. AUTONOMIC: loss of bladder/bowel control, sexual dysfunction. All functions lost at and below the level of lesion.
keyConcept: Complete transection: initial spinal shock (flaccid) → later spastic paralysis, total sensory and autonomic loss below lesion

explanation: Brown-Sequard syndrome (hemisection of cord): IPSILATERAL to lesion: UMN paralysis below level, loss of conscious proprioception and fine touch (dorsal columns), LMN signs at exact segment level; CONTRALATERAL to lesion: loss of pain and temperature starting 1-2 segments below (spinothalamic fibers have already crossed). At lesion level: LMN signs at that specific level.
keyConcept: Brown-Sequard: ipsilateral UMN paralysis + dorsal column loss; contralateral pain/temperature loss

explanation: Anterior spinal artery occlusion: AREA AFFECTED is the anterior 2/3 of spinal cord. CLINICAL features: bilateral loss of motor function (anterior horn involvement) → flaccid then spastic paralysis; bilateral loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic tracts); PRESERVED: dorsal column functions (proprioception, vibration, fine touch) bilaterally since posterior columns are spared.
keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery occlusion: anterior 2/3 cord affected, motor + pain/temperature lost, dorsal columns preserved

explanation: Syringomyelia causes dissociated sensory loss: (1) BILATERAL cape-like loss of pain and temperature (due to damage to crossing spinothalamic fibers in anterior white commissure where syrinx forms); (2) Touch sensation partially preserved (dorsal columns intact); (3) Proprioception preserved; (4) Loss begins in upper limbs and may extend. The key finding is dissociated sensory loss - loss of pain/temperature with preserved touch and proprioception.
keyConcept: Syringomyelia: cavitation near central canal damages crossing spinothalamic fibers causing dissociated sensory loss

explanation: This case describes syringomyelia: a cavitation (syrinx) in the central part of the spinal cord. The patient has bilateral cape-like sensory loss. The pain and temperature fibers are involved because the crossing fibers in the anterior white commissure are closest to the central canal where the syrinx forms. Dorsal columns are spared. The most common site is cervical and upper thoracic segments where the central canal is widest.
keyConcept: Syringomyelia: cavitation damages closest crossing pain/temperature fibers; spares dorsal columns

explanation: This case describes normal anatomy during lumbar puncture: The correct lumbar puncture site is just above or below the L4 spinous process (L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspace). The spinal cord normally ends at the lower border of L1 vertebra in adults. The meninges terminate at: Dura and arachnoid end at S2; Pia mater continues as filum terminale to the coccyx. These are safe landmarks because the cauda equina floats freely in the subarachnoid space below L1.
keyConcept: Lumbar puncture site (L3-L4/L4-L5), cord ends at L1, meninges end at S2 (except pia)

explanation: This case describes a UMN lesion of facial nerve: Upper facial muscles are preserved because the upper part of the facial nucleus receives corticonuclear fibers from BOTH cerebral hemispheres (bilateral representation). Lower facial muscles are affected because they receive mainly contralateral input. The parasympathetic nuclei are superior salivary nucleus (submandibular, sublingual glands), special lacrimatory nucleus (lacrimal gland), and nucleus of tractus solitarius. The terminal branches are temporal, zygomatic, buccal, mandibular, and cervical.
keyConcept: UMN facial palsy spares forehead (bilateral cortical input), affects lower face; CN VII has 5 terminal branches

explanation: The ventral surface of the medulla oblongata shows: (1) PYRAMIDS - containing corticospinal fibers, located on either side of anterior median fissure; (2) OLVES (inferior olivary nuclei) - lateral to pyramids; (3) CRANIAL NERVES: CN IX (glossopharyngeal), CN X (vagus), CN XI (accessory - cranial part), and CN XII (hypoglossal) attach at the pontomedullary junction. The pyramids are most prominent features and are where pyramidal decussation occurs caudally.
keyConcept: Ventral medulla: pyramids, olives, and cranial nerves IX, X, XI, XII attached at pontomedullary junction

explanation: The ventral surface of the pons shows: (1) BASILAR SULCUS - midline groove containing basilar artery; (2) TRANSVERSE FIBERS - connecting the two hemispheres of cerebellum; (3) CRANIAL NERVES: CN V (trigeminal) attaches at the lateral aspect of the pons; CN VI (abducens), CN VII (facial), and CN VIII (vestibulocochlear) attach at the pontomedullary junction. The pons is divided into basilar part (ventral) and tegmental part (dorsal).
keyConcept: Ventral pons: basilar sulcus, transverse fibers, CN V at lateral surface, CN VI-VIII at pontomedullary junction

explanation: The ventral surface of the midbrain shows the cerebral peduncles (crura cerebri): two cylindrical masses separated by the interpeduncular fossa. CN III (oculomotor) emerges from the medial surface of each peduncle. The peduncles contain descending motor fibers. The midbrain connects the pons (below) to the diencephalon (above). The ventral midbrain is separated from the dorsal tectum by the cerebral aqueduct.
keyConcept: Ventral midbrain: cerebral peduncles with CN III emerging medially; connects pons to diencephalon

explanation: The interpeduncular fossa is bounded: ANTERIORLY by the optic chiasma; LATERALLY by the cerebral peduncles; POSTERIORLY by the mammillary bodies; INFERIORLY by the pons. CONTENTS: (1) Posterior perforated substance (contains central artery of midbrain); (2) Basilar artery bifurcation; (3) Mamillary bodies form the posterior boundary. It is a clinically important space for aneurysms and tumors.
keyConcept: Interpeduncular fossa: bounded by optic chiasma anteriorly, cerebral peduncles laterally, mammillary bodies posteriorly

explanation: The dorsal surface of the medulla oblongata shows: (1) INFERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLE - connects medulla to cerebellum; (2) MIDDLE CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLE - visible at the pontomedullary junction; (3) FLOOR OF FOURTH VENTRICLE: divided into MEDULLARY TRIGONE (containing hypoglossal trigone over hypoglossal nucleus and vagal trigone over dorsal motor nucleus of X) and PONTINE TRIGONE. The gracile and cuneate tubercles (over dorsal column nuclei) are visible above the trigone.
keyConcept: Dorsal medulla: inferior/middle cerebellar peduncles, hypoglossal and vagal trigones in fourth ventricle floor

explanation: The dorsal surface of the pons forms the upper part of the floor of the fourth ventricle: (1) FACIAL COLLICULUS - elevation over abducens nucleus and facial nerve fibers internally; (2) TRIGEMINAL TUBERCLE - over the principal sensory nucleus of CN V; (3) MEDIAL EMINENCE - longitudinal elevation; (4) SUPERIOR and INFERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLES form the lateral boundaries of the fourth ventricle at this level.
keyConcept: Dorsal pons: facial colliculus, trigeminal tubercle, forms upper fourth ventricle floor with peduncles as lateral borders

explanation: The dorsal surface of the midbrain (tectum) shows the quadrigeminal plate (corpora quadrigemina): (1) SUPERIOR COLLICULI - visual reflexes (paired); (2) INFERIOR COLLICULI - auditory pathway. Below the inferior colliculi are the superior cerebellar peduncles. The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only cranial nerve to exit dorsally, emerging between the two inferior colliculi.
keyConcept: Dorsal midbrain: quadrigeminal plate (superior and inferior colliculi); CN IV exits dorsally

explanation: The roof of the fourth ventricle has two layers: (1) SUPERIOR MEDULLARY VELUM - connects the superior cerebellar peduncles, contains lingula and central lobule of cerebellum; (2) INFERIOR MEDULLARY VELUM - stretches between the two inferior cerebellar peduncles; (3) The fastigium marks the apex of the roof. The roof is completed by the cerebellar vermis and its white matter. Choroid plexus protrudes through the lateral apertures.
keyConcept: Fourth ventricle roof: superior and inferior medullary vela, fastigium (apex), cerebellar vermis

explanation: The floor of the fourth ventricle (rhomboid fossa) has two regions: MEDULLARY TRIGONE: (1) Hypoglossal trigone (over hypoglossal nucleus) - elevation near midline; (2) Vagal trigone (over dorsal motor nucleus of vagus) - lateral to hypoglossal; (3) Area postrema - at the lower angle. PONTINE TRIGONE: (1) Facial colliculus (over abducens nucleus and facial nerve); (2) Locus coeruleus - pigmented neurons with norepinephrine.
keyConcept: Fourth ventricle floor: hypoglossal and vagal trigones (medulla), facial colliculus and locus coeruleus (pons)

explanation: The lateral boundaries of the fourth ventricle: (1) SUPERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLE - forms the upper lateral boundary; (2) MIDDLE CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLE - forms the lateral boundary at mid-pontine level; (3) INFERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLE - forms the lower lateral boundary; (4) FLOOR of lateral recess. The lateral apertures (foramina of Luschka) are located at the lateral extremities. The peduncles connect the cerebellum to the brainstem.
keyConcept: Fourth ventricle lateral boundaries: superior, middle, and inferior cerebellar peduncles at different levels

explanation: Structures seen in the floor of the fourth ventricle: (1) HYPOGLOSSAL TRIGONE - over hypoglossal nucleus (somatic efferent, CN XII); (2) VAGAL TRIGONE - over dorsal motor nucleus of X (visceral efferent); (3) AREA POSTREMA - chemoreceptor trigger zone; (4) FACIAL COLLICULUS - over abducens nucleus (somatic efferent, CN VI); (5) TRIGEMINAL TUBERCLE - over principal sensory nucleus of V; (6) LOCUS COERULEUS - noradrenergic neurons.
keyConcept: Fourth ventricle floor: hypoglossal trigone, vagal trigone, facial colliculus, trigeminal tubercle, locus coeruleus

explanation: There are four major lemnisci in the brainstem: (1) MEDIAL LEMNISCUS - from dorsal column nuclei (gracile/cuneate) through medulla, pons, midbrain to VPL thalamus; carries conscious proprioception and fine touch; (2) SPINAL LEMNISCUS - from spinothalamic tracts to VPL; carries pain and temperature; (3) TRIGEMINAL LEMNISCUS - from trigeminal sensory nuclei to VPM; carries face sensation; (4) LATERAL LEMNISCUS - from cochlear nuclei to inferior colliculus; carries auditory information.
keyConcept: Four lemnisci: medial (proprioception/touch), spinal (pain/temperature), trigeminal (face sensation), lateral (hearing)

explanation: Internal features of the medulla oblongata include: (1) PYRAMIDS - containing corticospinal fibers, located on either side of anterior median fissure; (2) OLVES - containing inferior olivary nuclei; (3) INTERNAL ARCUATE FIBERS - decussating sensory fibers from dorsal column nuclei; (4) MEDIAL LEMNISCUS - formed after sensory decussation, ascends through brainstem; (5) CRANIAL NERVE NUCLEI: hypoglossal, dorsal motor nucleus of X, nucleus solitarius, nucleus ambiguus, inferior salivary nucleus; (6) INFERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLES laterally.
keyConcept: Medulla internal features: pyramids, olives, internal arcuate fibers, medial lemniscus, cranial nerve nuclei

explanation: Pyramidal decussation: LOCATION at the caudal medulla where the medulla transitions to the spinal cord. PROCESS: About 85-90% of corticospinal fibers cross obliquely in the anterior median fissure. RESULT: Crossed fibers form the lateral corticospinal tract in the lateral white column; uncrossed fibers remain as the anterior corticospinal tract. CLINICAL: This decussation explains why unilateral cerebral lesions cause contralateral motor deficits.
keyConcept: Pyramidal decussation: 85-90% of corticospinal fibers cross at caudal medulla to form lateral CST

explanation: Sensory decussation (lemniscal decussation): LOCATION at the caudal medulla (similar level to pyramidal decussation). PROCESS: Second-order neurons from gracile and cuneate nuclei send fibers that become internal arcuate fibers and cross in the medulla. RESULT: These crossed fibers form the medial lemniscus which ascends to the contralateral thalamus. IMPORTANCE: This explains why dorsal column lesions cause ipsilateral sensory loss.
keyConcept: Sensory decussation: dorsal column nuclei fibers cross to form medial lemniscus; dorsal column lesions cause ipsilateral loss

explanation: Nuclei in the medulla oblongata include: (1) HYPOGLOSSAL NUCLEUS (somatic efferent) - in floor near central canal, supplies tongue muscles; (2) DORSAL MOTOR NUCLEUS OF X (visceral efferent) - parasympathetic to thoracic/abdominal viscera; (3) NUCLEUS AMBIGUUS (special visceral efferent) - motor to pharynx/larynx; (4) INFERIOR SALIVARY NUCLEUS (visceral efferent) - parasympathetic to parotid; (5) NUCLEUS SOLITARIUS (visceral afferent) - taste and general visceral sensation; (6) SPINAL NUCLEUS OF V (general somatic afferent); (7) COCHLEAR and VESTIBULAR NUCLEI; (8) GRACILE and CUNEATE NUCLEI; (9) ACCESSORY CUNEATE NUCLEUS.
keyConcept: Medullary nuclei: hypoglossal, dorsal motor X, nucleus ambiguus, inferior salivary, nucleus solitarius, cochlear/vestibular nuclei

explanation: The inferior olivary complex consists of: (1) MAIN OLIVARY NUCLEUS - folded gray matter receiving input from red nucleus, spinal cord, and cerebral cortex; (2) MEDIAL ACCESSORY OLIVARY NUCLEUS; (3) DORSAL ACCESSORY OLIVARY NUCLEUS. OUTPUT: Olivocerebellar fibers cross and enter cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle. FUNCTION: Involved in motor learning, coordination, and timing. Lesions cause intention tremor.
keyConcept: Inferior olivary complex: main, medial accessory, dorsal accessory nuclei; olivocerebellar fibers via inferior cerebellar peduncle

explanation: Structures in the basis pontis include: (1) LONGITUDINAL FIBERS - corticopontine, corticospinal, corticobulbar fibers descending through the pons; (2) TRANSVERSE FIBERS - pontocerebellar fibers linking the pons with the cerebellum (these are interrupted by longitudinal fibers); (3) PONTINE NUCLEI - gray matter between fiber bundles receiving cortical input; (4) BASILAR ARTERY runs in the basilar sulcus. The basis pontis is separated from tegmentum by the trapezoid body.
keyConcept: Basis pontis: longitudinal fibers (corticospinal), transverse fibers (pontocerebellar), pontine nuclei

explanation: Structures in the tegmentum pontis include: (1) CRANIAL NERVE NUCLEI: Abducens nucleus (CN VI), Facial nucleus (CN VII), Vestibular nuclei (CN VIII), Cochlear nuclei (CN VIII); (2) TRACT: Medial longitudinal fasciculus; (3) LEMNISCI: Medial lemniscus, trigeminal lemniscus; (4) NUCLEI: Superior olivary nucleus (sound localization), nuclei of reticular formation; (5) TRAPEZOID BODY (auditory pathway); (6) The pyramid does NOT continue here (interrupted by transverse pontocerebellar fibers).
keyConcept: Tegmentum pontis: CN VI, VII, VIII nuclei, medial lemniscus, superior olivary nucleus, reticular formation

explanation: The midbrain has three parts: (1) TECTUM (quadrigeminal plate) - dorsal, contains superior colliculus (visual reflexes) and inferior colliculus (auditory relay); (2) TEGMENTUM - between tectum and crus cerebri, contains crus cerebri, substantia nigra, red nucleus, RAPPORT decussation, medial lemniscus, and decussations of superior cerebellar peduncle and red nucleus; (3) CRUS CEREBRI (cerebral peduncle) - ventral, contains descending motor fibers (frontopontine most medial, corticospinal/corticobulbar middle, parieto/temporopontine most lateral).
keyConcept: Midbrain parts: tectum (colliculi), tegmentum (red nucleus, substantia nigra), crus cerebri (descending fibers)

explanation: The crus cerebri contains somatotopically organized descending fibers: MEDIAL 1/5 (most medial): Frontopontine fibers (from frontal lobe to pontine nuclei); MIDDLE 3/5: Corticospinal fibers (arm fibers anterior, leg fibers posterior) and corticobulbar fibers; LATERAL 1/5: Parietopontine and temporopontine fibers (from parietal and temporal lobes to cerebellum via pontine nuclei). The corticospinal fibers are somatotopically organized.
keyConcept: Crus cerebri: medial frontopontine, middle corticospinal/corticobulbar, lateral parieto/temporopontine fibers

explanation: Tegmental decussations of the midbrain include: (1) DECUSSATION OF SUPERIOR CEREBELLAR PEDUNCLE - dentate nucleus output to thalamus crosses in midbrain; (2) DECUSSATION OF RED NUCLEUS (rubrobulbar and rubospinal tracts) - crosses just below superior colliculus; (3) TROCHLEAR NERVE DECUSSATION - CN IV is unique as the only cranial nerve to exit dorsally and completely cross before emerging. These decussations are part of the extrapyramidal motor system.
keyConcept: Tegmental decussations: superior cerebellar peduncle, red nucleus, and trochlear nerve (only dorsal-exiting CN)

explanation: Nuclei of the vagus nerve: (1) DORSAL MOTOR NUCLEUS (GVE) - parasympathetic preganglionic fibers to thoracic and abdominal viscera (via thoracic vagal branches); (2) NUCLEUS AMBIGUUS (SVE) - motor to pharynx and larynx via pharyngeal branch and recurrent laryngeal nerve; (3) NUCLEUS SOLITARIUS (SVA/GVA) - taste from epiglottis and general visceral sensation; (4) SPINAL NUCLEUS OF V (GSA) - general sensory from larynx.
keyConcept: Vagus nerve nuclei: dorsal motor (GVE), nucleus ambiguus (SVE), nucleus solitarius (SVA/GVA), spinal V (GSA)

explanation: Nuclei of the glossopharyngeal nerve: (1) NUCLEUS AMBIGUUS (SVE) - motor to stylopharyngeus muscle (elevates pharynx); (2) INFERIOR SALIVARY NUCLEUS (GVE) - parasympathetic to parotid gland via otic ganglion; (3) NUCLEUS SOLITARIUS (SVA/GVA) - taste from posterior one-third of tongue and visceral sensation; (4) SPINAL NUCLEUS OF V (GSA) - general sensation from middle ear, pharynx, and posterior tongue.
keyConcept: Glossopharyngeal nuclei: nucleus ambiguus (stylopharyngeus), inferior salivary (parotid), nucleus solitarius (taste), spinal V (sensation)

explanation: Nuclei of the facial nerve: (1) FACIAL MOTOR NUCLEUS (SVE) - motor to muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior belly of digastric; (2) SUPERIOR SALIVARY NUCLEUS (GVE) - parasympathetic to lacrimal gland (via greater petrosal nerve and pterygopalatine ganglion), submandibular and sublingual glands (via chorda tympani and submandibular ganglion); (3) NUCLEUS SOLITARIUS (SVA) - taste from anterior two-thirds of tongue via chorda tympani; (4) MESENCEPHALIC NUCLEUS OF V - proprioception from facial muscles.
keyConcept: Facial nerve nuclei: motor (facial expression muscles), superior salivary (lacrimal, submandibular, sublingual glands), solitarius (taste)
